meta.phase: 2 of 2 - SETTLEMENT from primary sources. Every item was read in the PDF named in that item.
meta.scope: H2 (Das), H5 (Yuan), the measurement anchors src/sigma_anchor.py depends on, X-C18 (Ezuma/Guvenc), plus the Zhang decomposition our anchor docstring borrows.
meta.rule: A claim needs (a) exact PDF path, (b) which version, (c) the quoted sentence or table cell. Missing any one -> UNVERIFIED.

verdict_vocabulary.VERIFIED: the quoted sentence or table cell is in the named PDF at the named page
verdict_vocabulary.VERIFIED_BY_RENDER: the value lives in a table with NO text layer; the page was rendered at 650-750 dpi and the cell read visually. Weaker than a text extraction - flagged here, not hidden.
verdict_vocabulary.VERIFIED_AS_EVIDENCE: records evidence bearing on an open question, not a settled fact
verdict_vocabulary.REFUTED: the paper, or the filesystem, says something different from what we assert
verdict_vocabulary.PARTIAL: part of our assertion holds, part must be re-scoped
verdict_vocabulary.UNVERIFIED: no sentence in the primary source supports it, in either direction

H2_Das.verdict: VERIFIED, with three scoping corrections and three open questions
confirmed: IEEE WCL vol.15, pp.3731-3735, 2026, DOI 10.1109/LWC.2026.3705634 - published and peer-reviewed, not a preprint (A1).
Multiband monostatic AND bistatic, 1.8-27 GHz, seven bistatic angles 0:15:90 deg (A3, A6).
mu(f) = 0.21 f - 19.19 dBsm, DJI Phantom 3, theta_b = 0 - the exact coefficient src/sigma_anchor.py uses, read off the rendered Table III (A2).
Platform DJI Phantom 3, Table I 'Dimension' 35 cm x 20 cm, band 1.8-18.2 GHz which strictly contains our 1.843-5.21 GHz (A5).
The mean IS defined as a LINEAR azimuth average in section III-1, verbatim (A7).
corrections: POLARISATION: Das does not state it for the Phantom 3. Its one 'vertically polarized' sentence is scoped to the Phantom-2 setup, the only data Das measured. Cite Yuan section II-A instead (A9).
PROVENANCE: Das attributes the Phantom 3 data to its reference [7] (Wang et al., China Communications), not to our Yuan PDF (A10).
BISTATIC CONTENT: for the Phantom 3 the seven bistatic columns share one slope and one eps and differ by 0.63 dB of intercept in total (A18).
open: Das contradicts its own section III-1 in section III-2 (A8); the convention is NOT settled by the primary sources (C3 vs C4) and our +2.5068 dB conversion is a bet (C5).
Whether the Phantom 3 fit pools elevation cuts: unstated, the word is absent from the paper (A12).
What K the Phantom 3 fit used: the stated K = 360 fits only the Phantom 2 (A13).

H5_Yuan.verdict: VERIFIED in full, including the two slopes the ledger said we had never asserted
confirmed: EuCAP 2025, DOI 10.23919/EuCAP63536.2025.10999912, IEEE Xplore - published conference paper (B1).
Monostatic 3D UAV RCS in an anechoic chamber, CATR far-field (B4, B11).
Same airframe as Das: DJI Phantom 3, horizontal diagonal 35 cm, height 20 cm (B3).
VV polarisation, stated, with the paper's own caveat that all polarisation states should ideally have been measured (B5).
corrections: The elevation-sides sentence is in section II-A, pdf page 2 - the ledger's Y03 cites section III-A (B4).
Bistatic is explicitly Yuan's future work; Yuan gives us no bistatic anchor (B11).
open: Yuan never defines its mean statistic beyond 'the mean value in dBsm'; our 'linear azimuth mean' label is OUR inference (B7).

Das_vs_Yuan_statistic_mismatch.brief_framing: eps about 0.08 dB (Yuan) vs about 5.2 dB (Das) for a comparable platform cannot be the same quantity.
Das_vs_Yuan_statistic_mismatch.settlement: Right conclusion, wrong premises on all three counts. (1) The platform is not 'comparable' - it is the SAME DJI Phantom 3, same laboratory, near-certainly the same raw sweep (C1). (2) Yuan's eps is not in dB at all: the paper prints no unit and Fig. 5's right axis is an unlabelled 'Standard deviation' running 0 to 0.25; Das's eps is captioned '[DB]' (B8). (3) They are different quantities because Yuan's eps is the spread parameter of a Rician fit on a linear amplitude scale while Das's is a dB-domain standard deviation whose magnitude matches the 5.570 dB theoretical value for a Rayleigh-amplitude target (C3).

the_real_mismatch_is_in_mu_not_eps.note: The two papers summarise one measurement 3.23-3.59 dB apart at our three bands. That gap - not the eps difference - is what our anchor level depends on, and no sentence in either paper explains it.

items.topic: Anderson-Darling formula and the Phantom 3 goodness-of-fit
items.version: IEEE WCL eq.(5) and section III-2
items.page: eq.(5) journal p.3733 ; the 0.436 on p.3734
items.quote: d_AD( sigma^AAV(theta_b,f_i), F_xi(x) ) = -K - (1/K) sum_{k=1}^{K} (2k-1) x [ ln( F_xi(sigma^AAV(theta_b,f_i,phi_k)) ) + ln( F_xi(sigma^AAV(theta_b,f_i,phi_{K+1-k})) ) ] || For these platforms, the Rician distribution achieves the lowest mean dAD, namely 0.532 and 0.436, respectively.
items.note: 0.532 is the Mini 2, 0.436 the Phantom 3. Log-normal is best for the M350 RTK (4.11) and the Phantom 2 (1.04). Das reports only the winner per platform, so rcs_anchor.json's 'Gamma/LogNormal individual values not in the note' remains true of the paper itself.

items.topic: Kaiser window and the calibration constant
items.version: IEEE WCL sections II-2 and II-3b
items.quote: A metallic cylinder with radius 5.5 cm, height 30 cm, and known RCS sigma_Cal = 2.8 dBsm is placed at the center of the turntable || range gating is applied to the background-free range profiles using a sixth-order Kaiser window
items.note: sigma_Cal enters eq.(3) as a bare scalar with no frequency or bistatic-angle argument, so 'constant across all frequencies and bistatic angles' is a correct reading of the equation.

items.target: ledger D08 / how we cite Das as bistatic support
items.topic: Das's Phantom 3 / Mini 2 / M350 bistatic columns carry almost no information
items.version: IEEE WCL Table III and section IV-4
items.quote: Changing from monostatic to bistatic (90 deg) geometry increases the mean path-loss by only about 1-2 dB, indicating that frequency- and platform-dependent RCS variations dominate over bistatic-angle effects in this setting.
items.note: For the three re-used platforms the slope is bit-identical across all seven theta_b and eps does not move at all; only the intercept slides monotonically, 0.62-0.63 dB in total. The one platform with genuine bistatic structure - non-monotonic, slope-varying, 3.43 dB span at 15 GHz - is the Phantom 2, the dataset Das actually measured. CONSEQUENCE: Das is titled mono AND bistatic, but for OUR anchor airframe the bistatic content is 0.63 dB of intercept. Citing Das as bistatic support for a passive-bistatic study overstates it.

items.target: the brief's H5 framing and the Das-vs-Yuan epsilon mismatch
items.topic: Yuan's epsilon is NOT in dB - the '0.08 dB vs 5.2 dB' comparison is between incommensurable quantities
items.quote: Fig. 5 caption: 'Rician fitting results, including (a) the mean and standard deviation of the measured and Rician-fitted RCS and (b) the distribution parameters.' Right-hand axis label on all three panels: 'Standard deviation', with unitless tick ranges 0-0.25 (theta=90), 0-0.15 (theta=0), 0.04-0.14 (theta=180).
items.brief_said: 'their eps is about 0.08 dB against Das's about 5.2 dB for a comparable platform, which cannot be the same quantity.'
items.settlement: Right conclusion, wrong premises. (1) Not 'comparable' - it is the SAME airframe, DJI Phantom 3, 35 x 20 cm, in both papers, and near-certainly the same measurement (C1). (2) Yuan's epsilon carries NO unit; the paper never writes dB for it and the figure axis is unlabelled. Das's epsilon is captioned '[DB]' in the Table III caption. So Yuan's epsilon is not 0.08 dB - it is 0.08, dimensionless as printed. Calling it dB is itself an error. (3) They differ because Yuan's epsilon is the spread parameter of a RICIAN fit on a linear amplitude scale (Yuan measures that fit's K factor at -8.9 to -62.8 dB, i.e. nearly Rayleigh), while Das's epsilon is a dB-domain standard deviation whose 5.21-5.71 dB magnitude matches the theoretical value for a Rayleigh-amplitude target within 6 percent (C3).
items.action: Never place Das epsilon and Yuan epsilon in one column. sigma_anchor.py's EPS_UNITS block already says this - keep it and cite this item.

items.topic: CvM distances and normalised percentiles
items.quote: The average CVM distances for the Rician, Gamma, and LogNormal distributions are 0.28, 0.31, and 0.48, respectively. || the normalized RCS power shows probabilities of 10% and 1% below -8.5 dBsm and -18.5 dBsm under favorable conditions (i.e., with dominant scattered components), respectively. In contrast, for poor-sensing conditions (i.e., lacking dominant components), the corresponding power thresholds are -10 dBsm and -20 dBsm.

items.topic: Yuan's Swerling labelling
items.quote: this paper illustrates how the Rayleigh distribution (Swerling III/IV) inadequately models UAV RCS, as depicted in Fig. 6.
items.note: Our characterisation of the quote is exact, so the criticism (a Rayleigh amplitude corresponds to Swerling I/II) is safe to state - but state it as our reading of a parenthetical, and note that two sentences later the same paper writes the ungrouped and correct form: 'the exponential and Rayleigh distributions (the foundational distributions for Swerling I-IV) are specific instances of the Gamma and Rician distributions'.

items.topic: Are Das's Phantom 3 numbers the same measurement as Yuan's?
items.version: Das Table I + acknowledgment ; Yuan section II-A
evidence_for: Das Table I's Phantom 3 column and Yuan section II-A agree on every field both state: 35 x 20 cm, 1.8-18.2 GHz, 2801 frequency points, azimuth -90:2:90, far-field, anechoic.
Das's acknowledgment credits Prof. Wei Fan of Southeast University for the Phantom 3 data; Wei Fan is Yuan's corresponding author and Yuan's affiliation is Southeast University.
evidence_against: Das cites reference [7] (Wang et al., China Communications 2026) as the source, not Yuan's EuCAP paper.
A third paper by the same group exists (Das [8] = Yuan et al., IEEE AWPL 24:222-226, 2025 = Yuan's own [15]). We hold neither [7] nor [8].
items.settlement: Same airframe and same laboratory: proven. Same raw dataset: highly likely, stated by neither paper. Independent replication: definitively NOT - our anchor rests on one airframe measured by one laboratory.
items.action: Keep the 'single platform / single lab' uncontrolled term; reword it per A10.

items.topic: The Das-Yuan level gap, recomputed from verified coefficients
items.note: Our stated 3.23 / 3.41 / 3.59 dB gap and the 3.13 / 3.19 / 3.25 dB log-normal conversion both reproduce exactly. This is OUR derivation across two papers, not a statement either paper makes - it must always be labelled so.

items.topic: Evidence that Das's mu is a dB-DOMAIN mean, despite section III-1
lines: Das section III-2's log-normal remark states mu = E[10log10 sigma] and eps = std(10log10 sigma) outright (A8).

Table III's eps is captioned '[DB]'. For the Phantom 3 it runs 5.21-5.71 dB over the measured band and for the Mini 2 5.49-5.74 dB. The theoretical std of 10log10(sigma) for exponential sigma is 5.5700 dB. A dB-domain standard deviation is the only reading under which the eps column has a natural meaning - a LINEAR azimuth mean has no companion 'standard deviation in dB'.

reconcile_das_yuan() over 1.8-18.2 GHz: the exponential offset +2.5068 dB leaves residual RMS 0.238 dB and absmax 0.489 dB against Yuan's elevation-pooled linear mean; the log-normal offset +3.4322 dB leaves RMS 0.853 dB and absmax 1.177 dB.

Das's own best fit for the Phantom 3 is Rician (A16) and Yuan measures that fit's K factor at -8.9 to -62.8 dB, i.e. essentially Rayleigh amplitude - exactly the regime in which +2.5068 dB (10/ln10 times Euler's gamma) is the correct constant.
items.note: Three independent lines favour the dB-domain reading.

items.topic: Evidence that Das's mu is a LINEAR azimuth mean
lines: Section III-1 defines it that way in an equation, verbatim (A7). It is the paper's only explicit definition and it is unambiguous.
Fig. 3's caption calls the fitted quantity 'the mean and standard deviation of the measured monostatic RCS' - i.e. the III-1 quantity is what was fitted.
Fig. 2(a)'s caption calls the plotted quantity the 'Angle-averaged mean RCS'.
items.note: One line of argument, but of the strongest kind: the authors' own defining equation.

items.topic: 'RESOLVED_EMPIRICALLY' overstates what the primary sources support
items.we_said: status = 'RESOLVED_EMPIRICALLY', with 0.925 dB (the gap between the two candidate conversion constants) carried as the only leftover uncertainty.
items.settlement: The residual minimisation that 'resolves' it rests on two assumptions that neither paper states: (i) Yuan's mu is a linear azimuth mean - the paper gives no definition at all (B7); (ii) Das's Phantom 3 fit pools Yuan's three elevation cuts - the word 'elevation' does not occur anywhere in Das (A12). Drop (ii) and compare Das against Yuan theta=90 alone and the gap is 3.23-3.59 dB, which NEITHER candidate constant explains. The reconciliation is therefore not a measurement of Das's convention; it is a fit with two free structural choices, weighed against the paper's own defining equation (C4).
items.why_it_matters: Taking Das at its section III-1 word would remove 2.5068 dB from the anchor level for EVERY airframe.
items.action: Downgrade the status to UNRESOLVED / EVIDENCE_SPLIT and enlarge the carried uncertainty from 0.925 dB (constant-vs-constant) to the full 2.507 dB (convert-vs-do-not-convert). The +2.5068 dB may still be the better bet - C3 gives three reasons - but it is a bet.
